grammar_points.name: 〜たら (tara: if; when)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add たら (tara) to the past tense form (た-form) of a verb to create a conditional — 'if/when X happens'. It's the most common and versatile conditional form.

Example from this song: 歩いたら (aruitara) = 'if/when you walk' — from 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩いた (aruita, past) + ら (ra) = 歩いたら (aruitara)

More examples:
• 見る (miru, 'to see') → 見たら (mitara, 'if you see')
• 着く (tsuku, 'to arrive') → 着いたら (tsuitara, 'when you arrive')
• いい天気 (ii tenki, 'nice weather') → いい天気だったら (ii tenki dattara, 'if the weather is nice')

Note: たら often implies discovering something: 開けたら猫がいた (aketara neko ga ita, 'when I opened it, there was a cat'). It's the go-to conditional for beginners — it works in almost any situation.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 歩く (aruku, 'to walk') → 歩いた (aruita, past) + ら (ra) → 歩いたら (aruitara, 'if/when you walk')

grammar_points.name: 〜のままに (no mama ni: as it is; following)

explanation.en:
How it works: Use noun + のままに (no mama ni) to express following something without resistance — 'as X dictates' or 'following the flow of X'. まま means 'as is' and に indicates manner.

Example from this song: 衝動のままに (shoudou no mama ni) = 'following the impulse / as the impulse dictates' — from 衝動 (shoudou, 'impulse') + の (no) + ままに (mama ni, 'as is')

More examples:
• 心 (kokoro, 'heart') → 心のままに (kokoro no mama ni, 'following your heart')
• 気持ち (kimochi, 'feeling') → 気持ちのままに (kimochi no mama ni, 'as your feelings dictate')
• 流れ (nagare, 'flow') → 流れのままに (nagare no mama ni, 'going with the flow')

Note: ままに implies surrendering control and letting something guide you. Without に, まま means the state remains unchanged: そのまま (sono mama, 'as it is').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 衝動 (shoudou, 'impulse') + の (no) + ままに (mama ni, 'following') → 衝動のままに (shoudou no mama ni, 'following the impulse')

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative form)

explanation.en:
How it works: Change the verb ending to create a direct command. For -u verbs (godan), change the final syllable to its え-row equivalent. For -ru verbs (ichidan), replace る with ろ.

Example from this song: 笑え (warae) = 'Laugh!', 泣け (nake) = 'Cry!', 叫べ (sakebe) = 'Shout!', 走れ (hashire) = 'Run!' — a series of commands rallying the listener.

More examples:
• 歌う (utau, 'to sing') → 歌え (utae, 'Sing!')
• 生きる (ikiru, 'to live') → 生きろ (ikiro, 'Live!')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しろ (shiro, 'Do it!')

Note: This song stacks multiple imperatives for powerful effect. Each godan verb simply changes its ending: う→え, く→け, ぶ→べ, る→れ. This pattern is very common in motivational rock songs.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 笑う (warau, 'to laugh') → 笑え (warae, 'Laugh!') / 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣け (nake, 'Cry!') / 叫ぶ (sakebu, 'to shout') → 叫べ (sakebe, 'Shout!') / 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走れ (hashire, 'Run!')

grammar_points.name: 〜かな (kana: I wonder)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add かな (kana) at the end of a sentence to express wondering or uncertainty — 'I wonder if...' It's softer and more reflective than か (ka) alone.

Example from this song: 差すかな (sasu kana) = 'I wonder if it shines through' — from 差す (sasu, 'to shine/point') + かな (kana, 'I wonder')

More examples:
• 大丈夫 (daijoubu, 'okay') → 大丈夫かな (daijoubu kana, 'I wonder if it's okay')
• 来る (kuru, 'to come') → 来るかな (kuru kana, 'I wonder if they'll come')
• いい (ii, 'good') → いいのかな (ii no kana, 'I wonder if it's alright')

Note: かな is used when talking to yourself or thinking aloud. Adding の before かな (のかな) adds more of an explanatory nuance. かな is gender-neutral, while かしら (kashira) is the traditional feminine equivalent.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 差す (sasu, 'to shine') + かな (kana, 'I wonder') → 差すかな (sasu kana, 'I wonder if it shines through')

grammar_points.name: 〜くらい (kurai: to the extent of)

explanation.en:
How it works: Add くらい (kurai) or ぐらい (gurai) after a word to express degree or extent — 'so much that' or 'to the point of'. It quantifies the intensity.

Example from this song: 痛いくらい強い (itai kurai tsuyoi) = 'strong to the point of being painful' — from 痛い (itai, 'painful') + くらい (kurai, 'to the extent of') + 強い (tsuyoi, 'strong')

More examples:
• 泣く (naku, 'to cry') → 泣くくらい嬉しい (naku kurai ureshii, 'so happy I could cry')
• 死ぬ (shinu, 'to die') → 死ぬくらい好き (shinu kurai suki, 'I like it so much I could die')
• 一時間 (ichijikan, 'one hour') → 一時間くらい (ichijikan kurai, 'about one hour')

Note: くらい has two uses: 1) expressing extent/degree (this song), 2) expressing approximation — 'about/approximately'. Context makes the meaning clear.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 痛い (itai, 'painful') + くらい (kurai, 'to the extent of') + 強い (tsuyoi, 'strong') → 痛いくらい強い (itai kurai tsuyoi, 'strong to the point of pain')

grammar_points.name: 〜てる (teru: progressive contraction)

explanation.en:
How it works: In casual speech, 〜ている (te iru, progressive/resultative) is shortened to 〜てる (teru). This is extremely common in everyday Japanese and in songs.

Example from this song: 生きてる (ikiteru) = 'is living / is alive' — from 生きている (ikite iru, 'is living') → contracted to 生きてる (ikiteru)

More examples:
• 食べている (tabete iru, 'is eating') → 食べてる (tabeteru)
• 知っている (shitte iru, 'knows') → 知ってる (shitteru)
• 待っている (matte iru, 'is waiting') → 待ってる (matteru)

Note: This contraction happens in all tenses: てる (present), てた (past = ていた), てない (negative = ていない). Understanding this contraction is essential for understanding casual Japanese and song lyrics.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 生きている (ikite iru, 'is living') → 生きてる (ikiteru, 'is alive' — casual contraction)
